name: Estonia
summary_text: Same-sex sexual activity is legal throughout Estonia for both men and women. It was re-legalized on 1 June 1992 after restoration of independence, the specific criminal provision was removed in 2001, the age of consent was equalized in 2002 at 14 and was raised in 2022 to 16 for all persons.  Same-sex couples can marry and jointly adopt. The marriage equality bill passed on 20 June 2023 by 55 to 34, was signed on 27 June by President Alar Karis and took effect on 1 January 2024, with the first marriage recorded on 2 January. Estonia is the first formerly Soviet-occupied state and the only Baltic country to legalize same-sex marriage. Opposition filed more than 700 amendments to block the bill and all failed. Registered cohabitation has been available since 1 January 2016 under the Registered Partnership Act passed by 40 to 38 and signed by President Toomas Hendrik Ilves.  Legal gender recognition has been available since 1992, with the first correction of name and gender on a birth certificate recorded on 6 April 1992 through a medical expert committee. The current framework rests on the Common Requirements for Medical Operations for Gender Reassignment in force since May 1999 and parts of the Vital Statistics Registration Act in force since January 2014, originating in a decree of 24 April 1997. The process remains medicalised and requires a psychiatric or mental-health diagnosis. Hormone therapy has not been mandatory since February 2022, genetic testing is not required, surgical intervention has not been required since April 1997 though it is permitted one year after the directive, and there is no forced sterilization. No nonbinary marker is recognized. Advocacy continues for recognition based on self-determination, and ministerial intent stated in May 2023 envisages change based on self-identification with correct markers for non-binary people.  Estonia approved a national LGBT+ equal-opportunities action plan in 2025, developed over about two years by the Equality Policies Department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications and approved by Economy Minister Erkki Keldo. It sets targets across education, healthcare, employment and legal-framework reform, with special attention to trans wellbeing. Its trans-relevant commitment is to update the legal framework to support protections for gender identity and expression. A December 2025 account records adoption of the plan to strengthen LGBTI equality across education, healthcare, employment and the legal system.  Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. Sexual orientation discrimination in employment was banned from 1 May 2004 through transposition of an EU directive and by the Equal Treatment Act in force on 1 January 2009, which covers employment but not goods and services. Gender identity discrimination is treated as implicitly prohibited in all areas through the Gender Equality Act since 1 May 2004, interpreted to extend to transgender and non-binary people and to cover less favourable treatment in connection with other circumstances related to gender and gender-based harassment. Sources differ on housing, with one recording protection for sexual orientation only and another recording workplace, housing and healthcare protections as including gender identity.  There are no hate-crime protections recorded as covering sexual orientation or gender identity in one dataset, and hate speech and hate crime legislation is recorded as not including gender identity in another. The Penal Code since 2006 prohibits public incitement to hatred based on sexual orientation, with paragraph 151 requiring danger to life, health or property. A June 2023 draft to explicitly ban hate speech passed first reading in September 2023. Advocacy continues for hate-speech and hate-crime laws. Conversion therapy is recorded as not banned. Bathroom access is recorded as protected. There is no censorship, and LGBTI organizations can register.  Official protection signals are consistent. The Foreign Minister publicly supported Tallinn Pride and missions flew rainbow flags. Estonia joined 16 EU states urging Hungary to revise its anti-LGBTI laws. Foreign embassies and international missions in Tallinn issued a joint declaration for Baltic Pride 2017 held in Tallinn on 6 to 9 July, affirming LGBTI rights as human rights. An LGBT+ Community Support Group was formed in the Riigikogu in May 2023, chaired by openly gay Eduard Odinets. Courts awarded damages in February 2017 for failure to adopt partnership implementing acts and ruled in May 2019 that Rakvere City Council’s 80 percent funding cut to the Festheart LGBTI festival was unlawful. After the homophobic assault at X-Baar on 11 June 2023, police arrested and charged serious breach of public order with possible deportation, as confirmed by Interior Minister Lauri Läänemets.  Violence risk remains documented. In the EU Fundamental Rights Agency 2024 country sheet, 62 percent avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner compared with 53 percent for the EU-27, 40 percent avoid certain locations for fear of assault compared with 29 percent, 38 percent are open about being LGBTIQ compared with 51 percent, and reported work discrimination at 12 percent was below the EU average of 19 percent. Participants in the 2007 pride were verbally and physically attacked and no parade was held until 2017. On 14 July 2023 a court sentenced a Russian-speaking man to 12 years for the 2022 murder in Tallinn of a Jamaican trans woman met in a Tallinn Old Town bar, who was stabbed more than 34 times while trying to flee. The court imposed a harsh sentence for severity and rejected a provocation claim, noting she had asked his friend to tell him she was transgender and whether he was comfortable with intercourse a second time.

name: Fiji
summary_text: Private adult consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful in Fiji since 1 February 2010, when the Crimes Decree 2009, cited as the Crimes Act 2010, took effect and repealed the historic Penal Code offence under Article 175. That offence had carried a maximum penalty of fourteen years imprisonment.  In April 2005 two men, Australian tourist Thomas McCosker and Fijian man Dhirendra Nadan, received two-year prison sentences under Article 175 for consensual sex. The trial judge described the acts as so disgusting that any decent person would vomit. Human Rights Watch called for the charges to be dropped and the men released, citing the 1997 constitutional prohibition on sexual orientation discrimination. The convictions were overturned in August 2005 by the highest court as a violation of the Constitution.  Enforcement ended in practice before repeal. In July 2006 the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested.  Fiji prohibited sexual orientation discrimination in its 1997 Constitution, the second such constitutional protection in the world after South Africa. That Constitution was abolished in 2009. The Constitution promulgated in September 2013 reinstated the protection and extended it. Article 26(3)(a) bans unfair direct or indirect discrimination on grounds including sex, gender, gender identity and expression and sexual orientation. In 2013 the Government also included sexual orientation and gender identity in anti-hate speech law and in law dealing with discrimination in certain businesses.  No legal route exists for a trans person to change a gender marker. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, despite the constitutional protection on gender identity and expression. A 2023 Asia Pacific Alliance policy brief and case study on legal gender recognition describes this as constitutional protection with zero implementation, resulting in documented marginalisation and discrimination.  Fiji recognises a traditional third-gender population known as vaka sa lewa lewa, people assigned male at birth who dress, act and behave as female. Sources describe this group as traditionally accepted by Fijian society. That acceptance has no legal effect.  Fiji provides no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions. The Marriage Act 2002 limits marriage to one man and one woman, with an express ban on same-sex marriage since 2002. Prime ministerial opposition was reaffirmed on 26 March 2013, in January 2016 and in 2019.  Lack of trust in police due to possible harassment likely discourages LGBTQ people from reporting anti-gay violence or hateful discrimination. Reports describe hate crimes as rare. Documented cases include the brutal murder in Suva on 1 July 2001 of Red Cross leader John Maurice Scott and his partner Gregory Scrivener in an apparent homophobic attack with a possible political motive, the brutal murder in Suva in May 2018 of a young transgender woman, and a gay student found dead in Nasinu in September 2017. Activists report that physical violence and domestic abuse operate as familial conversion therapy for many LGBTQ+ people.  Reports of societal discrimination and bullying are described as not uncommon. Social mores regarding sexual orientation and gender identity are described as conservative, with little public support for LGBTQ rights. Majority Methodist and Catholic denominations traditionally view transgender identities negatively. The Muslim minority, about 6% of the population, tends to view cross-dressing as sinful behavior that needs to be fixed. In April 2005 Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex and called homosexuality a sin in a conservative Christian nation, days after the two-year sentences noted above.  Public displays of affection are not illegal. Visitors are advised that such displays are generally considered offensive.  The Government has in the past cancelled gay pride marches. LGBTQ activists organised activities on 17 May 2013 for the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia, held an event in Suva in 2017 attended by activists and religious figures, and held Fiji's first pride parade on 17 May 2018 in Lautoka with local police escort and an address by former President Epeli Nailatikau.

name: Fiji
summary_text: Private adult consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful in Fiji since 1 February 2010, when the Crimes Decree 2009, cited as the Crimes Act 2010, took effect and repealed the historic Penal Code offence under Article 175. That offence had carried a maximum penalty of fourteen years imprisonment.  In April 2005 two men, Australian tourist Thomas McCosker and Fijian man Dhirendra Nadan, received two-year prison sentences under Article 175 for consensual sex. The trial judge described the acts as so disgusting that any decent person would vomit. Human Rights Watch called for the charges to be dropped and the men released, citing the 1997 constitutional prohibition on sexual orientation discrimination. The convictions were overturned in August 2005 by the highest court as a violation of the Constitution.  Enforcement ended in practice before repeal. In July 2006 the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested.  Fiji prohibited sexual orientation discrimination in its 1997 Constitution, the second such constitutional protection in the world after South Africa. That Constitution was abolished in 2009. The Constitution promulgated in September 2013 reinstated the protection and extended it. Article 26(3)(a) bans unfair direct or indirect discrimination on grounds including sex, gender, gender identity and expression and sexual orientation. In 2013 the Government also included sexual orientation and gender identity in anti-hate speech law and in law dealing with discrimination in certain businesses.  No legal route exists for a trans person to change a gender marker. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, despite the constitutional protection on gender identity and expression. A 2023 Asia Pacific Alliance policy brief and case study on legal gender recognition describes this as constitutional protection with zero implementation, resulting in documented marginalisation and discrimination.  Fiji recognises a traditional third-gender population known as vaka sa lewa lewa, people assigned male at birth who dress, act and behave as female. Sources describe this group as traditionally accepted by Fijian society. That acceptance has no legal effect.  Fiji provides no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions. The Marriage Act 2002 limits marriage to one man and one woman, with an express ban on same-sex marriage since 2002. Prime ministerial opposition was reaffirmed on 26 March 2013, in January 2016 and in 2019.  Lack of trust in police due to possible harassment likely discourages LGBTQ people from reporting anti-gay violence or hateful discrimination. Reports describe hate crimes as rare. Documented cases include the brutal murder in Suva on 1 July 2001 of Red Cross leader John Maurice Scott and his partner Gregory Scrivener in an apparent homophobic attack with a possible political motive, the brutal murder in Suva in May 2018 of a young transgender woman, and a gay student found dead in Nasinu in September 2017. Activists report that physical violence and domestic abuse operate as familial conversion therapy for many LGBTQ+ people.  Reports of societal discrimination and bullying are described as not uncommon. Social mores regarding sexual orientation and gender identity are described as conservative, with little public support for LGBTQ rights. Majority Methodist and Catholic denominations traditionally view transgender identities negatively. The Muslim minority, about 6% of the population, tends to view cross-dressing as sinful behavior that needs to be fixed.
